276.name: Tobar dhìreach
276.province: the high valleys, on the north side of the central mountains
276.history: Tobar dhìreach, the straight well, is the hearth of Clann a' Chlachair and the place where fire came to the hill-folk. The well it is named for runs along a straight channel cut in the rock, and the old telling says it was on this ground, in the dead of a winter, that Neachdan the mason set his wedge in a seam he had not seen and broke into a vein of hard coal that showed every colour in the break; that the lightning struck the broken vein that night and it took fire; and that he carried a burning piece home, and his household sat by the first fire any of them had seen. From that hearth the fire was begged and given, carried in a clay pot banked with ash to the near hearths and then to the far ones, until there was no hearth of the hill-folk that was not lit from it, by one borrowing or another. The vein burned in its cut through the lives of the mason's son and grandson and beyond, watched through the dark half of every year from two flat stones above it. When it burned out, Muirne of the line would not let it be dug further: a flat slab was laid over the broken vein, no water was drawn beside it, and the well was cut again a stone's throw off. The black well and the young well, in the valleys on either side, each tell that the mason's well was theirs; Tobar dhìreach can show the capped shaft with a scorched stain on its lip, and the other two have only the telling. No house stands beside Leac na Fèithe. The household keeps two things for the line: Poit an Teine, the clay pot said to hold the mason's first fire, kept alight by the women of the line from mother to daughter and aunt to niece; and a leather bag of coloured pieces broken from the vein before it was covered, with fresh pieces taken in each lifetime from where the vein shows in a stream bank above the well. Here Diarmad asked why the coal had colours, and came home from the grove with Aithris a' Chruthachaidh and Tòimhseachan a' Choimhdich; here the fathers' names are said standing on Oidhche an Dealanaich, and the lightings of the coals are told as they come: gold on the sea, the snowflake in the air, the black coal in the ground by Leac na Fèithe, the red-brown in blood, the silver in the river below the house, gual teine on the doorstone in Seathan's fingers. From the lifetime of Colla the line is called Clann na Ceiste by the valleys. At the close of the age some ninety souls live at Tobar dhìreach, and Ailean son of Suibhne has gone north to the grove with six fires on a pole, leaving Lìobhan and the child Gormshuil to keep the house fire until he comes home.
276.known_for: Teine a' Chlachair, Leac na Fèithe over the burnt vein, and the bag of na Seachd Guail

277.name: Àth gharbh
277.province: the high valleys, on the hill road east of Tobar dhìreach
277.history: Àth gharbh, the rough ford, lies a short walk from Tobar dhìreach on the hill road, where the burn runs broad and stony and the drovers rest their beasts. Its households are kin by marriage to half the high valleys, and it was here that the valleys about the crack came to call themselves by one name: at the gathering on Oidhche an Dealanaich, an old man of the western household answered a stranger's question with a word for the whole of the gathered valleys, Clann nan Dè, and the name was said the next year at hearths that had not been at the gathering. Rathnait, born in the valleys about the crack, lived long enough to hear it in ordinary use. The households of Àth gharbh lay their dead in the ground on their side, knees drawn up, facing the central mountains, with an uncut stone at the head. It was also at Àth gharbh that an gual dathach was first burned outside the line. Barabal, a woman of a household of the ford, dropped a sliver of it into her peat fire, and it burned black-flamed like any other coal, and the hearthstone round it was stained through with colour. Her husband's mother turned the stone over at the door in daylight and said she had heard Clann a' Chlachair kept coloured stones such as this. The stained hearthstone is shown to travellers who ask after it and to children who do not. At the close of the age the ford holds some twelve households, and the drovers' beasts still churn the burn to mud at its crossing.
277.known_for: the name Clann nan Dè and the first small burning outside the line

454.name: Achadh dhìreach
454.province: the high valleys, west of Tobar dhìreach
454.history: Achadh dhìreach, the straight field, holds the oldest hearths of the high valleys after the mason's own. Eachna, a young woman of a household near Tobar dhìreach, walked the level ground west of the well more than once, looking at it the way a woman looks at a thing she means to have, and in the end carried fire there in a clay pot and laid the first hearth of the place on stone, as the near hearths had learned to do. The hearths were of pine and heather charcoal, with scrapers of grey flint and the split bones of red deer about them; there was no coloured coal in them. Deer were hunted by torch across the straight field, and within a generation five hearths stood there. The first autumn store of roasted hazel-nuts on the island was put by at Achadh dhìreach, in a pit lined with bark. Late in the age the households of the straight field began to rub broken coal from the vein into the wool of their dead, and it took streaks of a colour no plant dye makes. Giorsal of Achadh dhìreach was the one who began it, after her grandmother had shown her a scrap of coloured stone kept in a box three generations and called only the bright stone; when Giorsal died, her daughter rubbed a sliver into her mother's own wrapping. It is seldom done, one grave in some thirty. At the close of the age some sixty souls live at Achadh dhìreach.
454.known_for: its oldest hearths and the stained wool of its dead

1001.name: Bothan nan Ròn
1001.province: Eilean mhin, off the southern coast
1001.history: Bothan nan Ròn, the seal bothies, is the camp of the seal-hunters on Eilean mhin. The hunters came to the island by boat, the first on the island known to have crossed open water of set purpose: Oisean, who built his boat of hide over a frame of hazel, and his brothers after him, and then the young men of the neighbouring households, until the crossing in the calm months was a thing the shore simply did. They pitched their bothies of hide and turf on the green above the landing, kept them a season at a time, and left them standing when they went home, to be patched and roofed again the next year. The seals of Eilean mhin haul out on the flat rocks below the camp, and the hunters take them there with clubs and spears. By the close of the age the bothies have been kept every season since Oisean's own, and the ground beneath them is black with the fires of every season.
1001.known_for: the first crossing of open water on purpose

1002.name: Bothan an Fhoghair
1002.province: the skerries off Eilean fhada, on the northern coast
1002.history: Bothan an Fhoghair, the autumn bothies, is the camp of the north-shore hunters on the landward point of Eilean fhada, opposite the skerries where the grey seals haul out to pup in the autumn gales. Hunters went out in skin boats in that weather, the worst of the year, because the seals are there then and at no other time. Scàire, who went out with her father's crew from her sixteenth year and was master of his boat after his death, kept the camp in her day, and no one on that coast doubted that she read a north-shore sea as well as any man alive on it. The seal bones in the middens of the northern shore bear the same cut-marks as those of the camp. The bothies are low huts of stone and turf, roofed with hide in the season and left bare in the rest of the year. At the close of the age the autumn crossing is still made by some dozen boats, though since the loss of the boats of Ros ruadh the hunters go out only when the gulls are on the water and come home before dusk.
1002.known_for: the autumn seal-hunt on the skerries

1004.name: Àirighean a' Bhealaich
1004.province: the high passes of the central mountains
1004.history: Àirighean a' Bhealaich, are the summer camps of the herders in the high passes of the central mountains, where the grass is sweet after the snow goes off it. Each household of the upland valleys keeps its own shieling there, a hut of stone and turf with a fold beside it, and goes up with its beasts when the lambs are strong enough to walk. Since the great cats of the mountains were first seen to keep their roads, crossing by fixed ways at fixed seasons, the households have learned the crossing season and keep off the passes while it lasts: the shielings stand stripped and shuttered at the same point in every year, and a crossing mark is cut on each gatepost and scraped when the season has been kept. A boy sent up to winter sheep in the crossing season, his father having lost the count of days in a wet spell, found his household's shieling already stripped by neighbours who had read the signs, and came down the same evening. The shielings are empty now in their season, and full in the rest of the summer.
1004.known_for: the shielings left empty while the cats cross

1005.name: Gleann nan Damh
1005.history: Gleann nan Damh, is the gully of the eastern woods into which the hill-folk of the east drive the red deer every autumn, along lines of stakes and brush set out through the trees, and kill them at the gully's throat with spears. The antlers of the greatest stags are stacked apart from the rest at the gully's mouth, and the stand of them grew higher every year. It was at the edge of Coille Naomh Muileann chiar above the glen that Sadhbh and two others first saw the white stag and none of them drew; afterward the hunters began letting the gully's beasts go when a pale one was among them, rather than risk the wrong one. Dubhghall drove the gully alone for the first time as a young man, threw wide at a young stag in his first year and practised all winter against a bundle of brush, and took the head of the drive when his uncle's knees would no longer hold him through a whole autumn morning; he was exacting in one thing only, that no young man should stand carelessly. At the close of the age the drive is kept every autumn by households from Cnoc fhionn to the edge of the woods.
1005.known_for: the autumn deer-drive and the stand of antlers

1006.name: Teallaichean a' Chladaich
1006.province: the southern shore, below the southern hills
1006.history: Teallaichean a' Chladaich, are the households of the hill-folk on the southern shore, a string of steadings on the slope above the beach, with barley in the small fields and boats on the shingle. They were lit from Teine a' Chlachair like every hearth of the hill-folk, carried south over the mountains in a pot. It was from here that a party of eleven, with Cairbre at their head, went up into the southern hills in the crossing season, the harvest inland having failed and the geese of the coast not yet gone over in their numbers, reading the season as a slow one. They did not come home. Cairbre's wife kept the twelfth day on the rise above the steadings, and the fourteenth and the twentieth, and by the thirtieth had stopped telling herself anything, and only watched. Their bones were found years afterward along the line the cats use, and were buried where they were found. At the close of the age the households of the shore keep the crossing season as strictly as any in the passes, and cut their gateposts deep.
1006.known_for: the eleven who went up in the crossing season

1007.name: Na Teallaichean Falaichte
1007.history: Na Teallaichean Falaichte, is the hamlet of the herders of the Doire uaine hills, a scatter of steadings in the folds of the hills south of Tobar dhìreach. The hill-folk found the rock faces of those hills cut all over with lines of signs, more than anywhere else on the island; Eimhir, a herder-girl following a strayed ewe up a defile before first light, found the first of them, and the elders judged the writing older than living memory. No one of the hills could read it; the tellings came to agree that it told of something that walked without breathing and fell upon any who lit a fire in its sight, and some lines were cut over and defaced by another hand. Dreams of the same shape came at several hearths, two herders saw a walker on the ridge and lived, and children went less often alone to the far pastures. Laoghaire dug the first pit-hearth, a fire under a slab at the foot of a slanting shaft bent near its foot so that no glow could climb it straight, with the smoke led out through a crack in the turf ten paces off. Other households dug the like, and within a few lifetimes the covered hearth was the hills' law. Eimhir kept her own hearth open to the last. At the close of the age no open fire shows in those hills.

1008.name: Achadh a' Chalbh
1008.province: the hill country south-west of Tobar dhìreach
1008.history: Achadh a' Chalbh, is the gathering-ground about Calbh Cnoc ghorm, the third of the standing stones of the saying, on a low rise in the hill country south-west of Tobar dhìreach. Ciannait, a woman of a nearby hearth, found the stone standing on the rise where she had never seen it, and put her hand to it; within two summers the rise had its name. The whole saying was said standing there for the first time, Cha do thàinig sinn; bha sinn ann, and an old woman said the sayings of the three stones together and said after them that the stone said in fewer words what Aithris a' Chruthachaidh had always said. The gathering was kept a second year and a third, and a market grew up at it, traders walking in from the northern shore with hides to trade for salt. In the years after Seathan's snap the crowd at the column grew to some hundreds on the nights of the great tellings; shelters were built about the stone and rebuilt many times, and one of Clann na Ceiste was sent to say the Line there, slowly, with a pause after each father's name long enough for it to be passed back to those at the back. At a great telling gual bogha-froise went round the crowd hand to hand through a whole night and came back at dawn as dark as it went. At the close of the age the hill country reckons its year by the gatherings at the column.
1008.known_for: the gatherings at the column and the saying said standing

1009.name: Bruthach nan Teaghlach
1009.history: Bruthach nan Teaghlach, is the scatter of hill-folk steadings along a long south-facing slope in the valleys of the south-east, above a river that runs down toward the coast of the kilns. The households came there from the high valleys in the lifetimes when the walls of the heights were being raised, herders looking for grazing that did not freeze, and they took the slope for its warmth and its springs. They were half a day's walk from Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh to the west, and some of their sick were carried there, and a day's walk from the empty platform of the temple in the hills to the north-east, which they did not climb. They keep a gathering of their own on Oidhche an Dealanaich, and send one of their elders to Tobar dhìreach in some years to hear the fathers' names said at the mason's hearth. At the close of the age some twenty hearths stand on the slope, and they lay their dead in the ground on the ridge above it, facing the central mountains.
1009.known_for: its warm south-facing slope and its many hearths

1010.name: Bothan a' Chaolais
1010.province: the strait of the north-western coast
1010.history: Bothan a' Chaolais, the bothies of the strait, is the seal-hunters' camp on the quiet water of the north-western strait, south of the headlands, where the tide runs slow between the mainland and the near skerries. The hunters of the north-west came here when they left the open water for fear of Uilebheist na Mara, working the lee of the headlands out of its sight; the seal bones thinned in the middens of the open coast and grew here, shell on shell and bone on bone, until the middens of the strait outgrew the old grounds. An old steersman of the strait said at a net-mending that the sea had not grown smaller, only that the island's hand had drawn back from the part of it a man could no longer trust. The camp is kept through the seal season and the autumn fishing, and some households of Ros ruadh winter there now. At the close of the age it is the busiest seal-camp of the north-west, and its boats do not go out past the point.
1010.known_for: the seal-hunt of the strait, out of Uilebheist na Mara's sight
